newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians urged to set up fund for "stolen" kids.
newsitem.headline: Australians urged to set up fund for "stolen" kids.

text.p: Australia's top human rights official on Thursday urged churches and community groups to set up a special fund to help thousands of Aborigines taken from their families, if governments rejected compensation demands.

Human Rights Commission president Ronald Wilson appealed to state and national governments to shun legal arguments and grant compensation out of moral obligation over a policy that his commission, in a landmark report this week, labelled genocidal.
Tens of thousands of Aboriginal children were taken from their parents under the forced assimilation policy, which began in the 1880s and did not end until the 1960s.
Wilson said only compensation and a national apology to the "stolen generation" could heal the wounds and move Australia towards racial harmony.
"We are convinced that resolving the hurts and the pain and suffering of the stolen generations ... must be resolved if reconciliation is to become a reality," Wilson told a news conference.

"The gross violations of human rights ... call for a major response in terms of reparation, which does not consist only of money, it consists of genuine acknowledgment, of apology, of restitution, of rehabilitation and, where appropriate, of money compensation."
The federal Liberal-National government has rejected calls for financial compensation, saying modern Australia could not take legal responsibility for the sins of past generations.
"Once a nation begins to go down that path, there is in fact no end," Prime Minister John Howard said on Wednesday.
But Wilson warned that Australia would be swept by a wave of litigation that could tie courts up for years if governments failed to act now.

And he urged ordinary Australians to join organisations involved in the taking of children, such as some churches, in donating to a national fund. Many of the Aboriginal children taken from their parents were put in Christian missions.
"This can be an upswelling of a desire to take the Aboriginal people to our hearts as honoured citizens of our country," he said.
The Human Rights Commission's 700-page report on the "stolen generation" catalogued a litany of physical and sexual abuse over decades.
Three state governments have formally apologised, but Howard has only made a personal apology, which Aboriginal leaders say is not enough. No government has moved to offer compensation.
